design_detail: Two linked analyses at 1.5 T with voxel-based morphometry (VBM8/SPM8, DARTEL, modulated gray-matter maps, 8 mm smoothing). (1) Cross-sectional comparison of three groups: 18 control non-smokers, 25 control smokers and 39 people with methamphetamine dependence who smoked cigarettes, scanned after 4–7 days of abstinence. (2) Longitudinal re-scan of 12 methamphetamine-dependent and 12 control participants over the first month of abstinence, testing group-by-time interactions. The design's point is to separate tobacco smoking from methamphetamine as an explanation for gray-matter differences.
can_establish: That some gray-matter differences previously attributed to methamphetamine (right orbitofrontal cortex, caudate) are also present in control smokers who do not use illicit drugs, and that other regional differences (superior temporal, parietal, precentral) distinguish the methamphetamine group from smoking controls; and, tentatively, that gray matter changed over the first month of supervised abstinence in the methamphetamine group but not in controls.
cannot_establish: Whether the remaining differences are caused by methamphetamine or precede use (no pre-use scan; no group of people using methamphetamine who do not smoke); what the gray-matter increase during abstinence means at tissue level (it could be inflammation or glial change rather than recovery); and whether any difference has a functional consequence (no cognitive or clinical outcome was measured).

sample.recruitment: Online and print advertisements at UCLA. Methamphetamine-dependent participants stayed as residents at the General Clinical Research Center with daily urine toxicology; control participants were outpatients tested at intake and each visit. About 60% of each longitudinal group had taken part in an earlier study from the same laboratory (Methods §2.2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 18–55. Excluded: central nervous system, cardiovascular, pulmonary or systemic disease, psychotropic medication, head trauma, HIV seropositivity, pregnancy, and any current Axis I diagnosis other than methamphetamine or nicotine abuse or dependence (SCID for DSM-IV). Smokers in either group had smoked on at least 25 of the previous 30 days; control non-smokers had smoked fewer than 5 cigarettes in their lifetime. People who had ever smoked more than 5 cigarettes, and methamphetamine-dependent people who did not smoke, could join the longitudinal but not the cross-sectional study, because only two methamphetamine-dependent participants were non-smokers (Methods §2.2).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (means with SEM). Cross-sectional: age 30.1 (2.2), 35.4 (1.8), 34.8 (1.5), F(2,79)=2.10, p=0.13; men 8 of 18, 13 of 25, 20 of 39 (chi-square 0.87); education 14.6 (0.4), 14.1 (0.3), 12.8 (0.3), F(2,79)=8.52, p<0.001, with the methamphetamine group lower than both control groups; mother's education 13.2, 13.6, 12.3, not significant (F(2,75)=1.74, p=0.18); alcohol days in the last 30: 2.4, 5.3, 5.4, not significant; cannabis days in the last 30: 0.1, 0.2, 1.1, p=0.01. Smoking did not differ between the two smoking groups (days used, cigarettes per day about 14 vs 13, pack-years about 11.5 vs 13.2, Fagerström about 3.8 vs 3.6, age of first cigarette; all p>0.2). Longitudinal: control 37.5 (2.3) and methamphetamine 33.8 (2.4) years old; 8 of 12 and 10 of 12 currently smoked; education 14.8 vs 12.7, p<0.005.
sample.attrition: Not stated for the cross-sectional study. For the longitudinal study only completers are described (12 per group); how many began and did not return, and how the 24 relate to the 82, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited volunteers; the methamphetamine group was studied as residents under supervised abstinence while controls were outpatients, so setting as well as drug status differs. People using methamphetamine who do not smoke are rare and were not recruited, so methamphetamine and tobacco cannot be fully crossed. Education was about 1.5 years lower in the methamphetamine group; the authors argue education is itself affected by use and point to similar maternal education.

exposure.measurement: DSM-IV dependence by SCID; Addiction Severity Index and a study drug-use survey; urine toxicology daily during residence for the methamphetamine group and at intake and each visit for controls (Methods §2.2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, Table 1: methamphetamine group used on 22.4 (SEM 1.3) of the previous 30 days, about 2.6 (0.4) g per week, 8.4 (1.3) years of heavy use (n=38) and 11.5 (1.5) years of use (n=33), first use at 21.7 (1.2) years. Longitudinal methamphetamine group: 21.1 days, 1.9 g per week, 6.8 years of heavy use, first use at 21.6 years. Route is not reported. Reported as study-sample characteristics.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco is the study's exposure of interest and was matched between the two smoking groups. Cannabis use was higher in the methamphetamine group (about 1.1 vs 0.1–0.2 days in 30) and was entered as a covariate; alcohol days did not differ; cannabis or alcohol abuse or dependence were exclusions. Other drug use is not described.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: First scan at 4–7 days of abstinence, verified by daily urine toxicology during residential admission. Second scan a mean of 23.5 days (SD 1.6) later in the methamphetamine group and 31.6 days (SD 13.1) later in controls (Methods §2.1).

comparison.controls: Two comparison groups: 18 lifetime non-smokers and 25 cigarette smokers, neither using illicit drugs beyond light alcohol or cannabis. The longitudinal control group was described as matched for smoking (8 of 12 current smokers against 10 of 12).
comparison.matching: Groups were similar in age, sex and alcohol use and, among smokers, in smoking history. Analyses covaried age, sex and cannabis frequency. Education was not a covariate in the main models; the authors report that adding it left results supported only at a more liberal uncorrected threshold of p<0.005.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; maternal education is the only premorbid proxy. The authors state explicitly that group differences may reflect premorbid risk factors.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Light alcohol or cannabis permitted; no illicit drug use; verified by urine testing.

outcomes.instruments: 1.5 T Siemens Sonata, T1 MPRAGE, 1 mm slices; VBM8 for SPM8 with DARTEL normalization, modulation without linear head-size scaling, 8 mm smoothing; gray-matter mask. A supplementary semi-automatic delineation of the caudate (FSL FIRST) was run for comparison with earlier volumetric studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: Modulated VBM intensity is a relative gray-matter volume index, not cortical thickness. No cognitive, behavioural or clinical outcome was measured in this paper.
outcomes.operationalization: Deficit was defined as a significantly smaller voxel-wise gray-matter value than a comparison group; change with abstinence as a significant group-by-time interaction with a within-group time effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Cross-sectional: voxel height p<0.001 with cluster-extent family-wise error correction at p<0.05, in a gray-matter mask. Longitudinal: voxel height p<0.001 uncorrected with a 100-voxel cluster extent and no family-wise correction (Table 3 footnote states uncorrected voxel-level p). So the recovery analysis is held to a weaker standard than the group comparison.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable for automated VBM; blinding is not reported for the supplementary caudate delineation.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reported only as cluster-level corrected p-values with cluster extents, peak F/T and Z values and MNI coordinates (Tables 2 and 3); no group means, SDs or percentage differences are printed, so standardized differences and overlap cannot be computed from the paper. Editors' calculation from peak T values (which are selected maxima and therefore upward-biased): control non-smokers versus the methamphetamine group, peak T 6.35 corresponds to about d=1.8; control non-smokers versus control smokers, T 5.59, about d=1.7; control smokers versus the methamphetamine group, T 5.10, about d=1.3. Cross-sectional findings: the three groups differed in bilateral orbitofrontal and precentral gyri, right frontal pole, left superior temporal and left superior frontal gyri. Control non-smokers had more gray matter than control smokers in one cluster only, the right orbitofrontal cortex (1043 voxels, p<0.001 corrected). Control non-smokers exceeded the methamphetamine group in ten clusters (right frontal pole/orbitofrontal, left orbitofrontal, left superior frontal, left insula, bilateral precentral, right middle temporal, right precuneus, left caudate, right cingulate). Control smokers exceeded the methamphetamine group in four clusters (left superior temporal, right inferior temporal, right supramarginal, left precentral); no region was larger in the methamphetamine group. The supplementary caudate delineation found smaller bilateral and left caudate in both smoking groups than in control non-smokers, with no difference between control smokers and the methamphetamine group. Measures of smoking and of methamphetamine use were not related to gray-matter values (no dose-response). Longitudinal: group-by-time interactions in bilateral superior temporal gyrus, right angular gyrus, right insula, left precuneus, left inferior frontal gyrus, left occipital pole and left cerebellum; within the methamphetamine group gray matter increased in those cortical regions between weeks 1 and 4 and decreased in the cerebellum, while no region changed in controls at the stated threshold.
analysis.covariates: Age, sex and frequency of cannabis use in all cross-sectional models. Not education (addressed only in a sensitivity analysis at an uncorrected threshold), not alcohol, not depressive symptoms (not measured here).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Directional hypotheses are stated in the Introduction (smaller prefrontal, cingulate and insular gray matter in both smoking groups; striatal and pallidal differences specific to methamphetamine), but there is no registration. The striatal hypothesis was not borne out in the predicted direction: the methamphetamine group's caudate was smaller, not larger, and did not differ from control smokers.
analysis.selective_reporting: The caudate result in the abstract combines a voxel-wise finding (methamphetamine versus control non-smokers) with a supplementary region-of-interest finding (control smokers versus control non-smokers); the supplement is a separate download. The longitudinal analysis is reported at an uncorrected threshold while the cross-sectional analysis is corrected.
analysis.power: Not formally reported. The authors name modest sample size as a limitation and note that the longitudinal sample is comparable to or larger than earlier within-subject imaging studies in this field.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After 4–7 days of abstinence, people with methamphetamine dependence who smoked had less gray matter than non-smoking controls in a wide set of regions, but compared with smoking controls the difference was confined to four clusters; the right orbitofrontal and caudate differences were as large in control smokers as in the methamphetamine group. Over the first month of supervised abstinence, gray matter rose in several cortical regions in the methamphetamine group and not in controls, on an uncorrected threshold, with the two groups rescanned after different intervals (about 24 versus 32 days).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that orbitofrontal and caudate deficits may be partly attributable to cigarette smoking or premorbid conditions, which the data support, and that the gray-matter increase with abstinence suggests some deficits are partly attributable to methamphetamine use, which is a weaker inference: it rests on an uncorrected longitudinal analysis in 12 per group with unequal scan intervals, and on regions that mostly did not differ from control smokers at baseline. The discussion is careful, naming premorbid risk, the absence of dose-response, and the possibility that an increase in gray matter reflects inflammation or reactive gliosis rather than repair. The claim to be first to show smaller parietal and caudate volume, and the inference that early deficits precede the expansion seen in long-abstinent samples, mixes cross-sectional comparisons across different studies.

timeline.event: Cingulate and hippocampal gray-matter deficits reported in people who used methamphetamine, with a largely smoking versus non-smoking group contrast (Thompson et al., 2004; appraised in this batch). This study did not reproduce the hippocampal finding, which the authors attribute to different methods.
Larger striatal volumes reported in long-abstinent samples (Chang et al., 2005; Jernigan et al., 2005, as cited), the opposite direction to the caudate finding here in early abstinence.
This study separates smoking from methamphetamine and finds the orbitofrontal and caudate differences also in control smokers.

replication.where_it_stands: Gray-matter differences in people who use methamphetamine are partly shared with tobacco smoking; the direction of striatal findings varies with abstinence duration across studies; longitudinal change during abstinence has been shown only once, at an uncorrected threshold, in 12 people.

funding.declared_conflicts: The senior author declares research support for projects other than this one under a UCLA contract (number 20063287) with Philip Morris USA (Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The declared tobacco-industry contract is recorded because this paper's conclusion assigns part of the gray-matter difference in people who use methamphetamine to cigarette smoking; the authors state the support was for other projects and the funders had no role. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, never a reason to discount the results. The senior author also authored the earlier Thompson et al. (2004) study whose hippocampal finding is not reproduced here.

what_would_settle_it: A four-group design with people who use methamphetamine and do not smoke (hard to recruit but decisive), or a prospective study scanning people before and after the onset of use, both with longer follow-up, corrected longitudinal statistics, equal rescan intervals and cognitive outcomes measured alongside the imaging.

key_findings.finding: Control non-smokers had more gray matter than control smokers in exactly one cluster, the right orbitofrontal cortex (1043 voxels, cluster-level p<0.001, family-wise corrected), and no other region differed between the two control groups.
key_findings.locator: Results §3.2; Table 2, Control Nonsmoker > Control Tobacco Smoker

key_findings.finding: Compared with control non-smokers, the methamphetamine group had less gray matter in ten clusters: right frontal pole/orbitofrontal (7314 voxels), left orbitofrontal, left superior frontal, left insula, bilateral precentral, right middle temporal, right precuneus, left caudate and right cingulate (all cluster-level p<0.05 corrected).

Compared with control smokers, the methamphetamine group had less gray matter in only four clusters (left superior temporal, right inferior temporal, right supramarginal, left precentral); no region was larger in the methamphetamine group.
key_findings.locator: Results §3.2; Table 2, Control Tobacco Smoker > Methamphetamine-Dependent Tobacco Smoker

key_findings.finding: A supplementary anatomical delineation of the caudate found smaller bilateral and left caudate volumes in both control smokers and the methamphetamine group than in control non-smokers (p<0.05), with no significant difference between the two smoking groups.
key_findings.locator: Results §3.2, final paragraph (Supplemental Results, Supplemental Table 1)
key_findings.note: The supplement is a .docx download and was not opened; the numbers behind this statement were not checked.

key_findings.finding: Neither smoking measures nor methamphetamine-use measures correlated with gray-matter values: no dose-response was detected.

Over the first month of abstinence, group-by-time interactions appeared in bilateral superior temporal gyrus, right angular gyrus, right insula, left precuneus, left inferior frontal gyrus, left occipital pole and left cerebellum; gray matter rose in those cortical regions in the methamphetamine group and fell in the cerebellum, while no region changed in controls.
key_findings.note: Table 3 is explicitly labelled uncorrected voxel-level p, with a 100-voxel extent; unlike the cross-sectional analysis, these results are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

key_findings.finding: The two longitudinal groups were rescanned after different intervals: a mean of 23.5 days (SD 1.6) in the methamphetamine group and 31.6 days (SD 13.1) in controls.
key_findings.note: Relevant to the group-by-time interaction, since the control group had the longer interval and still showed no change.

key_findings.finding: Groups did not differ in age, sex or alcohol use; the methamphetamine group had about 1.5 fewer years of education (F(2,79)=8.52, p<0.001) but maternal education did not differ (F(2,75)=1.74, p=0.18). The two smoking groups were comparable on cigarettes per day, pack-years and Fagerström score.
The authors did not reproduce the smaller hippocampal volumes reported by their own laboratory in 2004, attributing the difference to method.

Editors' calculation from the peak T values in Table 2 (upward-biased because peaks are selected maxima): about d=1.8 for control non-smokers versus the methamphetamine group, d=1.7 for control non-smokers versus control smokers, and d=1.3 for control smokers versus the methamphetamine group.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation d = T × sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2) at the peak voxel; the paper gives no means, SDs or percentage differences.

reporting_issues.issue: The cannabis ANOVA is given as F(2,79)=4.55, p=0.01 in the Results but as F=6.210, p=0.003 in the Table 1 footnote; the table marks the cannabis row with three asterisks while the footnotes define only one and two.
reporting_issues.consequence: The covariate's group difference cannot be verified as printed; p=0.0135 and p=0.0031 are the values implied by the two F statistics (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Two rows of Table 2 print identical T and Z values (right supramarginal gyrus 4.43/4.43; left precentral gyrus 4.24/4.24), whereas Z is below T in every other row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Transcription error in two of the four clusters that distinguish the methamphetamine group from control smokers, the comparison that carries the paper's main inference.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the left precuneus appears with coordinates −3, −60, 34 in the interaction list and −3, 60, 34 in the within-group list, and a cluster at x=−46 is labelled right frontal operculum.
reporting_issues.consequence: Coordinate or label errors; the anatomical attribution of two longitudinal clusters is unreliable.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that control smokers and the methamphetamine group both had smaller orbitofrontal and caudate gray matter than control non-smokers, but the caudate part of that statement comes from the supplementary region-of-interest analysis, not from the voxel-wise results where only the methamphetamine group differed in caudate.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the abstract would attribute to the main analysis a result that rests on a supplementary method.

reporting_issues.issue: The longitudinal analysis uses an uncorrected threshold with a 100-voxel extent, while the cross-sectional analysis uses family-wise cluster correction; the difference in standard is not discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence findings, which carry the recovery claim, are substantially less protected against false positives than the group differences.

reporting_issues.issue: How the 24 longitudinal participants relate to the 82 cross-sectional participants is not stated, and the longitudinal inclusion rules differed (non-smoking methamphetamine participants and ex-smokers were allowed).
reporting_issues.consequence: The degree of sample overlap, and whether the longitudinal methamphetamine group is representative of the cross-sectional one, cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: Education was excluded from the main models; the sensitivity analysis including it is reported only as supporting the results at a more liberal uncorrected threshold of p<0.005, without a table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the methamphetamine-versus-smoker differences survive adjustment for education at the paper's own corrected threshold is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: Years of use (11.5) is reported for 33 of 39 participants and years of heavy use (8.4) for 38, without explanation of the missing data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1 and footnotes b and c)
reporting_issues.consequence: Exposure duration rests on partial data.

domains.note: The study's design directly addresses the main confounder (tobacco) and covaries age, sex and cannabis; education still differs and is handled only in a sensitivity analysis, and premorbid differences cannot be excluded.
DSM-IV diagnosis with daily urine toxicology during residence; self-reported amounts incomplete for some participants.
Advertisement-recruited volunteers; residential versus outpatient participation differs with group; non-smoking methamphetamine participants could not be recruited.

The methamphetamine group lived in a research unit under supervised abstinence between scans, so the longitudinal change includes the effects of that environment; scan intervals differed between groups.
Attrition into the longitudinal sample is not described; several exposure variables have smaller n.
Automated VBM with a standard pipeline, identical for all groups.
Corrected statistics cross-sectionally but uncorrected longitudinally; the abstract merges a supplementary analysis into the main caudate claim.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is the methodologically strongest of the structural studies read in this batch: it adds the comparison group the earlier literature lacked, verifies abstinence, and reports that the orbitofrontal and caudate differences are shared with tobacco smoking. Its weaknesses are the absence of non-smoking participants who use methamphetamine, residual confounding by education, and a longitudinal analysis that is small, unequal in interval and uncorrected.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3427723 (accepted author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1–3 as text, both figure legends, acknowledgments, contributor and conflict statements; Figures 1–2 are statistical maps as images; the supplementary .docx with the caudate delineation methods and results was not opened because it is a download)
